compression.title: WikiWho
compression.lede: is the algorithm and API that attribute each word (token) of a Wikipedia article to the revision, and so the editor, that introduced it, with every removal and reintroduction (MediaWiki; README; provenance census).

sentences.text: WikiWho is "a service providing authorship attribution using a content persistence algorithm" (MediaWiki page), and its README states its function: "The WikiWho API gives access to the provenance/changes of words (tokens) in Wikipedia articles" (WikiWho README); the provenance census records the object it attaches provenance to as "a single token (word) of a Wikipedia article" (provenance census record).

The MediaWiki page heads it "A service that provides authorship attribution of Wikipedia articles" (MediaWiki page); the Meta research page states the aim "to provide an API for retrieving provenance and change information of single tokens in any arbitrary Wikipedia article revision", for every token "the revision of origin for that token, and all changes ever applied to it - with high accuracy" (Meta research page); its Wikimedia host calls it "A service for mining changes and interactions from revisioned writing platforms" (wikiwho.wmcloud.org).

The census files it under the lineage "authorship and reuse", its kind "algorithm and API", its capability as one that records and tests provenance, and its unit "a token in an article revision" (provenance census record).

The algorithm, published by Flöck and Acosta at WWW 2014 as "WikiWho: Precise and efficient attribution of authorship of revisioned content" (WikiWho README; the census dates the algorithm "WWW 2014"), "parses the complete set of all historical revisions (versions) in order to find out who wrote and/or removed and/or reinserted which exact text at token level at what revision" (WikiWho README; MediaWiki page).

For every token "its individual addition, removal, and reintroduction history becomes available" (MediaWiki page), with the revision it came from "and thereby which editor originally authored the word", and "individual tokens retain a unique ID" so that identical strings in different positions stay distinct (WikiWho README); the census names the relations carried, "origin (the revision and editor that introduced the token)", "deletion" and "reintroduction", on the carrier "the article's full revision history, re-parsed" (provenance census record).

The census records the operations tested as "every edit in an article's revision history" and what survived as "per token: when it entered, who wrote it, every removal and reinsertion; method evaluated at 95% on revision-rich articles" (provenance census record), after the README's and the MediaWiki page's "extensive evaluation resulting in 95% accuracy on fairly revision-rich articles" (WikiWho README; MediaWiki page).

The problem precedes the tool: the Meta research page cites de Alfaro and Shavlovsky, "Attributing authorship of revisioned content" (WWW 2013), holds that "the task of identifying the "correct" original author of a piece of text in a WP article is not trivial", and relies on a method "scientifically proven to perform at 95% percent precision", "higher than any other algorithm proposed for the task, as far as we can tell" (Meta research page); the census carries the sentence on the task as its precision note (provenance census record).

Its stated limit of scope: "It is implemented currently for Wikitext, but can run on any kind of text in principle (although tokenization rules might have to be adapted)" (WikiWho README); the census leaves "the WWW 2014 paper itself" unchecked (provenance census record).

On top of the core data "An additional set of APIs delivers special HTML markup for interface applications, e.g., the browser extension WhoColor" (WikiWho README): "the WhoColor API delivers annotated HTML of a wiki article that can be read by a browser" (MediaWiki page), and the userscript "creates a color-markup on the text, showing the original authors of the content, an author list ordered by percentages of the article written and additional provenance information" (WikiWho README), "a userscript that highlights selected text pieces in an article annotated with their provenance (author)" (Meta research page).

"The WhoColor API is what powers the Who Wrote That? tool as well as features within the Wiki Education Dashboard and Programs and Events Dashboard", and the page lists the "Tools powered by WikiWho": Who Wrote That?, XTools Authorship, XTools Blame, the two dashboards and the pywikibot.Page.authorship() method (MediaWiki page); Wikipedia records that Wikimedia's "Community Tech Team has released Who Wrote That? , a browser extension, for Mozilla Firefox" and for Chromium-based browsers (Wikipedia, GESIS article); the census gives "WhoColor" and "Who Wrote That?" as names of the entity itself (provenance census record).

Wikipedia's section has "WhoColor and whoVIS are in development.", a statement whose sources the section cites as "Retrieved 8 October 2022" (Wikipedia, GESIS article); the census gives the data access as "the WikiWho and WhoColor APIs" (provenance census record).

Its makers name further uses: the identification of conflict "still poses several open research questions -- answers to which the WikiWho data can offer", and an extension reads relations between editors "using "(re)delete" and "reintroduce" actions between editors to encode antagonistic and supporting actions" (WikiWho README); the data "can also be used for extracting disputes about content" (Meta research page); researchers developing and using it "also investigated the Gamergate (harassment campaign)", and Contropedia "is a related "platform for the real-time analysis and visualization of such controversies in Wikipedia"" (Wikipedia, GESIS article).
Its data are carried further in TokTrack, "A Complete Token Provenance and Change Tracking Dataset for the English Wikipedia" (Flöck, Erdogan and Acosta, 2017, cited in the WikiWho README).

"WikiWho was first conceived as a dissertation project at Karlsruhe Institute of Technology by Dr. Fabian Flöck" and "It was hosted, maintained and further developed at the Computational Social Sciences (CSS) department of GESIS – Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences" (wikiwho.wmcloud.org; the README's Contributors: "WikiWho was first conceived as a dissertation project at" Karlsruhe), "developed by Fabian Flöck and Maribel Acosta and hosted by GESIS" (Wikipedia, GESIS article); "It was first developed by the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology and GESIS – Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences" (MediaWiki page).

"In August 2021, it was moved to Wikimedia Cloud Services infrastructure and is now maintained and under further development by Community Tech and the Wiki Education Foundation", while the page's infobox names the group "Moderator Tools • Wiki Education Foundation" (MediaWiki page); its host reads "This is Wikimedia's WikiWho API service. The API and the WikiWho algorithms were originally developed by GESIS" (wikiwho.wmcloud.org); the census records the operator as "first developed by Karlsruhe Institute of Technology and GESIS; since August 2021 maintained by Wikimedia Community Tech and the Wiki Education Foundation", moved "2021-08" (provenance census record).

Wikipedia's section gives the transition at another date: "In 2021, Fabian Flöck planned to leave GESIS and shut down WikiWho sometime in 2022, however, a Wikimedia Foundation software engineer is working to migrate the infrastructure." (Wikipedia, GESIS article).

The README states "The WikiWho API is currently hosted at GESIS" and at Wikimedia, and "In the future, only Wikimedia will continue its support." (WikiWho README); "The WikiWho APIs and OpenAPI documentation may be found at https://wikiwho.wmcloud.org/" (MediaWiki page), where "Available APIs" lists 70 WikiWho and 70 WhoColor language endpoints (wikiwho.wmcloud.org); the census records the address "https://wikiwho.wmcloud.org/" and the lifecycle "active", "moved to Wikimedia Cloud Services in August 2021; the GESIS host is to give way to Wikimedia" (provenance census record).

Its languages stand at two dates: the Meta research page, last edited 5 June 2024, says "We currently offer the service in English, German, Turkish and Basque, with more languages planned." and "A beta version of the API is live and working for en.wikipedia.org, although we are working on the performance." (Meta research page); the MediaWiki page, last edited 15 July 2026, lists 71 "Currently supported wikis", 70 distinct, Swedish Wikipedia twice (MediaWiki page); the census, reading on "2026-10-29", carries the four languages as its earlier-state evidence, tags the Meta page as "an earlier state of the project", and leaves "the list of supported wikis today" unchecked (provenance census record).
The Meta page states its own standing: "This page documents a research project in progress" and "Information may be incomplete and change as the project progresses." (Meta research page).

English Wikipedia has no article for it: the name is a redirect, "Redirected from WikiWho", into the section "WikiWho" of the article on GESIS – Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences, which says WikiWho "parses the complete set of all historical revisions (versions) (of Wikipedia articles in different languages) in order to find out who wrote and/or removed and/or reinserted which exact text at token level at what revision" (Wikipedia, GESIS article).

The article carries the notice "This article may rely excessively on sources too closely associated with the subject" (January 2015), and the page was last edited on 13 September 2026 (Wikipedia, GESIS article).

The census reads every resource it records by one question, "What provenance does this system carry, through which operation, on whose assertion, with what evidence of survival?", with the MMRS fields "extended for provenance" and the rule "Every quote is verbatim from a saved source" (provenance census record).

At its exact name on Google's AI Overview on 2026-10-29, "Every sentence of the composition is about wikiHow", the Overview shown unexpanded with "the source chips inline with their counts, no card rail" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), the chips showing only their sites: "Wikipedia +3", "Fastly +1", "wikiHow +2", "wikiHow +1" (the chips as shown).

The registry states the innocent reading first, "The Overview takes the query as a near spelling of wikiHow and answers about wikiHow, sourced to Wikipedia and wikiHow's own pages", records "no 'showing results for' line and no statement that the query was read as another name", and holds that "the composition answers a different entity as if it were the one asked for" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

It records the entity absent, "no person, institution, identifier or page of WikiWho's; the persons and sources named are wikiHow's", and "WikiWho, the algorithm and API that attribute each word of a Wikipedia article to the revision and editor that introduced it, does not appear." (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

It reads the substitution against the entity's function, "WikiWho attributes authorship in Wikipedia at the level of the word", and "the instrument for crediting Wikipedia's writers is replaced by a more-retrieved name one letter away" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29), at a name Wikipedia itself redirects to WikiWho's section (Wikipedia, GESIS article).

It calls it "The cleanest erasure of the census", the entity's place "taken by a neighbour of higher retrieval weight, with no notice to the reader", and the census record "the disambiguation the composition did not make"; the record "landed on provenanceerasure.org the same day (commit 8a9f153) and no card cites it" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

Its finding sets the README beside the query, "The query is the entity's exact name", and it carries the operator's note with the paste as given: "wikiwho gets replaced - good disambiguation on this one, and theyll owe us:" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

CAP-1-01.quote: Every sentence of the composition is about wikiHow.

CAP-1-06.quote: Unlike the thirteen others, the paste is the Overview as shown, unexpanded: the query once, the source chips inline with their counts, no card rail.

CAP-1-08.quote: The innocent reading first. The Overview takes the query as a near spelling of wikiHow and answers about wikiHow, sourced to Wikipedia and wikiHow's own pages.

CAP-1-03.quote: The paste carries no 'showing results for' line and no statement that the query was read as another name; the composition answers a different entity as if it were the one asked for.

CAP-1-11.quote: The entity is absent: no person, institution, identifier or page of WikiWho's; the persons and sources named are wikiHow's.

CAP-1-13.quote: WikiWho, the algorithm and API that attribute each word of a Wikipedia article to the revision and editor that introduced it, does not appear.

CAP-1-04.quote: WikiWho attributes authorship in Wikipedia at the level of the word.

CAP-1-05.quote: At its own name the composition layer gives a how-to site sourced in part to Wikipedia; the instrument for crediting Wikipedia's writers is replaced by a more-retrieved name one letter away.

CAP-1-09.quote: The cleanest erasure of the census: the entity is absent from the composition at its exact name, and its place is taken by a neighbour of higher retrieval weight, with no notice to the reader.

CAP-1-10.quote: The census record, with its verbatim self-description from WikiWho's README, the MediaWiki page and the Meta research page, is the disambiguation the composition did not make.

CAP-1-12.quote: A baseline: the record landed on provenanceerasure.org the same day (commit 8a9f153) and no card cites it.

CAP-1-02.quote: The query is the entity's exact name; the record: 'The WikiWho API gives access to the provenance/changes of words (tokens) in Wikipedia articles' (its README), maintained since August 2021 by Wikimedia Community Tech and the Wiki Education Foundation.

CAP-1-07.quote: The operator's note with it: 'wikiwho gets replaced - good disambiguation on this one, and theyll owe us:'.
